review:
This game should have been huge and taken over the FPS scene. Now you've got another chance to try one of the best FPS games in years. 

Even when the hype fades and the multiplayer possibly dies down again, the single player is beyond worth it.

[b]HUGE DISCLAIMER[/b]
The Steam version of Titanfall 2 STILL REQUIRES ORIGIN. It has NO useful Steam integration whatsoever. It launches the game through Origin, and you can only invite friends through Origin. If you've already got Titanfall 2 on Origin, you may as well skip this. 

THAT SAID
Titanfall 2 is one of the greatest (if not [i]the[/i] greatest first person shooters of our generation. The game's four years old, I'm not sure I can say anything that hasn't been said before.  The story is short and sweet, and genuinely really really good. The multiplayer is the meat of this game, and it's fantastic. Movement is fast and fun, shooting feels great (I mean, these dudes made Modern Warfare, so), piloting a giant robot is sick as hell.

I don't know what to tell you. If you play FPSs and you've never tried Titanfall 2, you owe it to yourself to buy this game.

Don't hesitate to buy Titanfall 2, it is truly a master of its class.
I literally don't understand why anyone still plays Call of Duty in a universe where Titanfall exists.

[u]Warning:[/u] If you are looking to play multiplayer and you are using Intel 10th gen or newer, you will fail to establish a connection to the server unless you do this workaround:

[u]Windows:[/u]

1. Right click on "This Computer" then > "Properties". 
2. Once you are there find the setting "Advanced System Options" 
[u]NOTE:[/u] If the window is opened through the traditional control panel then it's gonna be on the left hand corner of the window, if you are accessing this through the newer settings application found on Windows 10 and higher, then it's gonna be on the right hand corner.
3. Go on the "Advanced" tab and find "Environment Variables...".
4.Once you are there, we are greeted with two fields, the upper one is for your user account, the second one is global for your entire OS. We need to edit the one affecting the entire OS. You have to click on "Create" and add the following entries:
[u]Variable Name: OPENSSL_ia32cap
Variable Value: ~0x20000000[/u]
5. You are now ready to play Titanfall 2. Just make sure to restart the game if it was still running in the process. I personally restarted my computer as well just in case.

[u]Linux:[/u]

[b]Tip: Keep in mind that you have to run the game in "Proton Experimental". Otherwise the EA launcher will keep crashing on startup.[/b]
1. Open Steam, find Titanfall 2 in your library, right click on it and go to "Properties"
2. Head to the "General" tab and find the section with "Launch Options" which should be located at the bottom
3. Paste this on the launch options field:
[u]OPENSSL_ia32cap=~0x20000000 %command%[/u]
[u]NOTE:[/u] Steam specific commands go after the "%command" separator, before it, specific to Linux commands only work. If you are looking to enter other Linux specific commands such as "mangohud", just separate them with an interval (spacebar).
4. You are now ready to play Titanfall 2. Just restart the game if an instance of it is already running.

For the uninformed, Titanfall 2 is the game that Respawn Entertainment made before they made Apex Legends. Everyone knows about Apex Legends at this point, right? Compared to this game, I have ten times more hours in Apex across Origin and Steam, spread across 4+ years and 18 seasons at the time of writing. Clearly, I like Apex a lot (or at least I used to, at any rate), and I'll probably continue to play Apex in some capacity for the foreseeable future, no matter how much it may abuse me. Titanfall 2 makes me regret spending that much time in what I now think is a vastly inferior game.

Titanfall 2 is so much better, so much more [i]fun[/i] than its follow-up, that it's kind of incredible. Like Apex, I played this game on Origin first, so I have about 250 hours total. I genuinely think that in those 250 hours of Titanfall 2, I had roughly as much fun as I had in about 2.5k hours of Apex Legends. This game is honest-to-god 10x more fun than Apex. I have yet to meet somebody who played this game and did not like it.

Alright, now I'm just gonna gush and ramble and critique for way too long. You can and probably should stop reading here, but if you want to understand why I was jerking this game off so hard, you might get some answers below.

This game truly has it all. A quality campaign, incredible PvP, and a hidden gem of a PvE mode. And in every mode, you will experience some of the best movement in any GAME, let alone shooter. Also in every mode: piloting giant robots. That shit is just plain cool. If you disagree, I respect your opinion, but I also think you are lame as fuck.


[b][u]Campaign[/u][/b]
The definition of short but sweet. A bit overrated, IMO, but man, it's still really good. Just packed with creativity, every level is unique in some way. Even the worst ones are still mostly enjoyable because of how good the movement and gunplay are. It's also a great training course for multiplayer pilot gameplay. My only complaint is that it absolutely does not prepare you for multiplayer titan combat. Your campaign titan may share loadouts with the multiplayer titans, but it otherwise functions very differently.

A word of warning: Do not play on the hardest difficulty on your first playthrough. If you are bad at games, it will be impossible and miserable. If you are good at games, it will be possible, but tedious and still a little miserable.


[b][u]PvP[/u][/b]
This is the main attraction. For every match that's a terrible experience, I have 10 that were joyrides from start to finish. I will admit that I still haven't played every mode, but pretty much all of the ones I tried have been at least decent. 90% of my PvP matches are in the 'main' mode, Attrition. Attrition is honestly kind of genius. The developers found an answer to the question, "Without making the lobby size huge, how can a military shooter still feel like an actual war?" Attrition is 6v6 TDM with giant robots and computer-controlled "fodder" units. I put that in quotes because the AI can fuck your shit up if you're not careful. Not a common occurrence, but it's always embarrassing when it happens. Adding titans and AI opens up a surprising amount of gameplay diversity. Bad at pilot combat? Farm AI until you can call down your titan. Bad at titan combat? Auto-Scorch with Assault Chip; use that sucker as bait. It'll pick up a few random kills, too. (I've heard Auto-Northstar can be lethal as well.) Bad at everything? Well, at least you respawn fast. (Can't say the same for Apex...)

Balance is pretty good, too. Some things are definitely much better than others (looking at you, CAR), but every weapon and titan can be broken, given the right situation. And *almost* (again, looking at you, CAR) every weapon and titan can be useless, given the wrong situation. Everything has at least a little counterplay. When the opposition is running some utterly joyless loadouts and making my match completely miserable, I often feel like I can turn the tide with a smart counterpick and a little strategy. Doesn't always result in a win, but it usually makes [i]some[/i] kind of impact.

Also, when you're starting out, run whatever the fuck you want. You will sometimes find people that will try to give you shit for playing certain weapons (e.g. CAR, Spitfire) or titans (e.g. Tone, Monarch). These things are, admittedly, annoying to fight and/or easy to use. You still shouldn't feel bad for using them. (Unless you are intentionally using them to piss people off. Don't do that unless they were toxic first, you little shitter, you.) Don't let these people talk down to you just because you want to learn without getting [i]entirely[/i] stomped. This game has a sky-high skill ceiling. If the opponent can't deal with you, they aren't very good to begin with.

On the flip side, try to avoid calling anything broken or no-skill before you've actually gotten a chance to use it. I know I've had my fair share of eye-opening moments...

Aside from that, I've found that toxicity is pretty low outside of weapon shaming. For every racial slur or salty insult I see, there are 5 chat messages that are just wacky nonsense. It's great. You'll even see a 'ns' sometimes. Crazy!

[spoiler]though i do sometimes wonder what is going through the minds of g100 players that still use the car[/spoiler]


[b][u]PvE[/u][/b]
[b]THIS SHIT IS ACTUALLY GOOD.[/b] Frontier Defense is severely underrated. I have yet to get deep into this mode, but so far, it's been a blast. Massacring clueless grunts, mowing down armies of titans, watching your own titan slowly become the most overpowered thing you've ever seen, barely scraping by on your last retry. (Yes, there are retries. Don't leave until the match is over! Unless you already knew that, and you're just a filthy ragequitter.) It's all good stuff. I find Easy a little [i]too[/i] easy, but Regular is great for some brainless fun with a little challenge. Hard is actually hard and makes me have to think for once. I am currently too afraid to play Master and Insane, but I hope to one day git gud and try those out.


[b][u]Price[/u][/b]
Okay, this doesn't fit with the other sections, but it bears mentioning. This game is on sale relatively often, and the discount is usually [b]deep.[/b] I got this game on Steam for $3, and I think I bought it on Origin for $5.


[b][u]"Why did you buy this game twice?"[/u][/b]
Yeah, I understand nobody gives a rat's ass about this. As you can clearly see, I'm not expecting anyone to read down this far (or read this review at all, for that matter). Congratulations on making it here! Anyway, this will take some explaining. If you're not aware, this game still runs through Origin (well, technically, it's the "EA app" now). When you buy and install it on Steam, it actually just installs Origin on your computer, and whenever you run it, Origin will launch (don't worry, it closes when you close the game). Yep, this game is so good that I was willing to pay $3 for it to install Origin for me.

A Masterpiece That Deserved Better

This isn't just another FPS - it's a testament to what gaming can be when innovation meets perfect execution. The tragic irony is that this gem was sacrificed by EA's catastrophic decision to release it between Battlefield 1 and COD: Infinite Warfare, essentially burying one of the greatest FPS games ever created.

The campaign, though brief, is absolutely stellar. The relationship between Cooper and BT-7274 is something special that stays with you long after the credits roll. Every level brings something unique to the table, with some of the most creative mission design I've ever experienced in an FPS.

The multiplayer is where this game truly shines - the fluid movement system, the perfect balance between pilot and titan gameplay, the satisfying gunplay - it all comes together to create something that no other game has managed to replicate. Even Apex Legends, while good in its own right, couldn't capture the magic that makes Titanfall 2 special.

It's bittersweet to see this masterpiece available for such a low price. While it's an absolute steal for new players, it's also a reminder of how this game was mishandled. The fact that we're getting Apex content instead of Titanfall 3 feels like a cruel joke to those of us who know just how revolutionary this series could have been.

To new players: You're in for a treat. To EA: You had lightning in a bottle, and you let it slip away.

alright, let me talk about this game.

I've been playing this game since the game was released on Origin, but I've bought one more package on Steam. because, it deserves it.

compared to the first Titanfall game, Titanfall 2 has made improvements and very persuasive experiences.

Level design of singleplayer is a masterpiece, continuous actions and puzzles will not let you get bored. It is completely polished as a game, every stage and its theme changes its color periodically.

story is wonderful, It may not be quite good if you are someone who want the game stories should have to tell something that meaning, but the story of this game is telling what exactly the developers wanna say. it is the relationship between the Pilot and the Titan.
through the campaign, the relationship between you and your titan is growing up from a collaborator to a companion, from a companion to the friend.

This game focuses on The relationship between The Pilot YOU and your TITAN. when you have finished the campaign, you would have deep affections to your titan. I will not talk too much about the story of singleplayer. because i want you feel it in yourself. I'm sure you will 100% enjoy how you grow up from a rifleman1 to a qualified Pilot with your titan friend. and finally you will know, you will understand what I've said in this review. and this relationship is intentionally keep showing as player experience in multiplayer.


after the campaign, you would be missing the titan friend accompanied while entire story. but your relationship is keep going on the multiplayer.

In Titanfall 1, player always have seen the world in first person view. when you are running when you are embarking, when you are executing enemy, in Titanfall 1, You were a Pilot and also were Titan. starting from a grunt, and becoming to titan machine. that was Titanfall 1. But in Titanfall 2, developers intentionally show your titans at your eyes. It is much like developers are saying, "Look at this. this is your titan."

when you are embarking, the camera changes its view third person, and shows how Pilot, you and your Titan binding each other. when you are executing enemy titans, the camera shows how badass you were and also your titan was. They show the thing, in a one screen, Pilot, you, and your titan both.


If i tell about the multiplayer game itself, titan battle became much more stick and solid. In Titanfall 1, you could freely change your titan loadouts. Chassis, weapons, kits, etc etc, but In Titanfall 2, your titans have their own weaponry system and abilities. it is like champions in MOBAs. Some people didn't like this changes because it seems like just limitations. but I think differently. In my thought, too much freedom brings less diversity lead to less freedom, because there is always most efficient loadouts exist in these type of games and it will dominate entire contents. it will make lack of contents compare to the actually prepared.
Titanfall 2 avoided this problem. Titan loadouts are more limited but actually these limitations make sense. it makes necessity of cooperation.
Whether you are skilled or not, you can not just dominate battlefield on your own. but with your teammates you can. because your titan unit clearly has weak-point, you should drive him/her much delicately. to maximize your advantages and minimize weakness. this feels very reasonable.

And there are titan kits. that offers little tweak-able aspects for your titans. titan loadouts are not completely fixed. by your kits, titans will be little more different. you can customize your play style enough. but I think it could update little more options like teamfortress 2 so that the game earns more longevity.

besides the titans have little limitations, pilot loadouts still ample.
there are various weapons you may have seen already at APEX Legends. Tactical Abilities are basically classes but your loadouts are not be restricted by that. weapons have there own signatures, so learning and researching how to use them is very interesting. Most people recommend CAR sub-machine gun because it is very basic and effective weapon, but ultimately, it depends on your playstyle.
Pilot versus Pilot combat is not like any FPS you have played. It is something like human size dogfight. so the outcome is not by aiming skill like twitch shooters. 


Titanfall 2 is most interesting FPS game I ever had played. I hope that, more people enjoy this game.

This game had the potential to be the standard of shooter games for years to come. Shooter games were PERFECTED here and instead the people chose hero shooters, tac shooters, BR’s, and whatever the hell CoD decides to release every year. The fact that this game exists is a slap in the face to all AAA shooter releases in the past 10 years, because the devs understood that games are for the players, and not a tool to suck the the most money possible out of the consumer.

For a whole THREE UNITED STATES DOLLARS (on sale) you get a complete and working campaign (wow how did we get to a point where that isn’t standard) that has incredibly unique level design and so many memorable moments. 

The multiplayer provides the one of the most unique and fun gameplay loops I’ve ever seen. The interaction between all of the games mechanics, including pilots, titans, ability and weapon customization, movement, and map design create a phenomenal experience throughout every match. No holding angles for 2 minutes straight, no being forced to swap off heroes because they instantly lose to another hero, no battle royale. You get to play how you want whenever you want and the game rewards that with pure speed, power, and an adrenaline rush like nothing else.

Also, this game has NONE of the predatory business practices that we see so often nowadays. There is a store (purely selling cosmetics) but its not shoved in your face constantly, there’s no battlepass, and an there’s extremely large amount of cosmetics that are completely free. 

Oh and, it looks great and runs great, even on older GPUs (perks of using the source engine)

So yeah if you’re tired of modern shooters and looking for something that makes you feel like a badass without the bullshit, pick up the greatest shooter games of all time for 3 dollars.

Single player review only.

So I'm just a few years late to the party, but this game has been on my radar ever since they announced a single player campaign...and it has a fantastic campaign at that. In can be finished in 6-ish hours or so, but it's one of those games that cut out all the fat without adding any filler and in the end the experience was totally worth playing. 

This game felt like a mix of Crysis, Transformers and Mirrors Edge. The weapons feel AMAZING, and I couldn't wait to try out a new one that popped up. Plus, every time you come across a
weapon not only does it show the name of it but also a short summary of what it does- very handy during intense combat. Double jumping around and wallrunning had me a little concerned at first but it felt natural (and fun)in no time. Moving on to the mech combat- its truly satisfying.  The premade loadouts you'll find through the campaign are all fun to try out to see what you like best and/or choose for the situation. And the story? Well, it's simple and straightforward, and like I said earlier- no filler. I loved it.

 The connection between my Titan and I felt very similar to The Terminator and John Connor in T2. Voice acting is all top notch and well written.

Like my Battlefield 1 review, this game also does the story extremely well without adding cliche scripted "epic" moments or ticking a box just to have a feature in the game. Since the game is made my ex members of Infinity Ward who also brought us CoD 4 Modern Warfare, it gave me that same feeling of being engrossed in the story and characters in almost every way.

As an avid FPS enjoyer, I have always heard good things about Titanfall. What for many years prevented me from playing it was my stupid ass thinking "no way I'm playing another CoD clone". I would like to take this opportunity to formally apologize to Respawn for fabricating such a thought in my mind. Compared to TF, CoD is an old and senile man's game. I’ll start my review with my take on the singleplayer campaign, as it’s not exactly what I expected from the creators of the modern military shooter genre. Instead of placing the player in the boots of a grunt who must follow their leader’s orders at all times, Titanfall 2 lets us be a badass Pilot who can dropkick someone in the face, then cloak and effortlessly wallrun across a massive gap and take out an annoying sniper, all in a few seconds. There are some scripted moments, but for the most part, Respawn Entertainment‘s first attempt at a singleplayer campaign is a rare sight in the modern videogame landscape, as the player can choose how to engage the enemy without being told that they are out of bounds or similar things.

The game’s story is a collection of cliches but it’s well told and the voice actors in charge of bringing both friends and foes to life do a great job. Those who didn’t play the original Titanfall won’t be lost here, although the new title references events that happened during the multiplayer campaign featured in the first game in the series. As a militiaman turned Pilot (Pilots are highly skilled special units who can call down Titans and possess superhuman movement abilities thanks to their high tech jump pack kits) we will have to fight our way through territory held by the evil Interstellar Manufacturing Corporation, trying to find a way to stop their oppressive regime from taking over the galaxy. As the game goes on, players will bond with their Titan, a hulking mechanical beast named BT-7274 who can’t stop saying unintentionally funny things. Just as in the multiplayer modes, game time will be divided between on-foot sections in which we’ll have to sneak and make use of our superhuman movement skills, and Titan battles in which we’ll have to engage similar sized threats (and boss Titans)

As I said previously, the on-foot sections are mostly freeform, with the player being provided with an objective and set loose upon huge levels. Although the majority of the campaign consists of gunfights separated by small environmental puzzles, there is a special level which reminded me of Portal and will probably stay fresh on my mind for years, thanks to the way in which it was presented and the freshness of the gameplay on display. Most sections revolve around a particular gimmick or thing to do for the player, and then drop it completely, ensuring that the game never feels repetitive. Aside from the variety in offer during the Pilot parts of the campaign, the combat is also fast paced and rewarding, letting you slide across the floor, wallrun and go invisible at the touch of a button all in the same combat encounter. Yes, most levels can be completed with tried and true tactics such as popping out of cover, hitting the enemy in the head with a few well placed rounds and then taking cover again, but the great thing about Titanfall 2 is that this is just one of many possible options. Other modern military shooters have adopted the wallrun and jetpack mechanics, but they still force players to hide behind cover once their health gets low, or to wait for specific scripted moments in order to continue onwards.

Titan combat scenarios are different, because they are mostly linear affairs in which the player must either fight hordes of robots, a few enemy Titans at the same time or a powerful boss Titan. Defeating bosses adds their loadout to the player’s inventory, and BT-7274 can swap weapons and abilities mid fight, something that can be incredibly useful during boss fights. The unlockable Titan loadouts also work as a sort of training for the multiplayer mode, since they are the same different chassis that can be used when battling online.

So, the campaign is great, but I hear you asking… How is the multiplayer mode? Is it as good as Titanfall 1 or did Respawn make a great singleplayer shooter with a weak multiplayer component? Is it even alive?

I hear you, multiplayer fans, and you can rest easy knowing that Titanfall 2′s online offering is not only a great game on its own, but it also isn’t just a rehash of the first game’s player versus player component with a few tweaks thrown in for good measure. Instead, Respawn Entertainment chose to revamp the entire concept, going from small tweaks such as the removal of Titan shields, to bigger changes like the addition of a grappling hook or the introduction of a completely new mechanic such as Titan Batteries. There are new game modes as well, such as the Pilots only variant (which disables Titanfalls) or the Coliseum, which pits one player against another in a match of sheer skill.

Matches start just as they did in the first title, with everyone running around as an agile Pilot, wallrunning all over the place and using different gadgets such as grappling hooks, sonar based knifes that can reveal the enemy’s position, stealth kits and other fun high tech tools. Killing enemy combatants advances the Titanfall timer, and once that meter is full, players can call down their mighty mechanical buddies. Just like in Titanfall 1, Titans can be set to be AI controlled or the player can climb inside and control them in real time. However, thanks to the removal of the shield system, AI mode titans are quite easy to kill, so they won’t be such a common sight as they were in the first game in the series. Another important change is the Battery system. Instead of rodeoing an enemy Titan and shooting at its core with a gun, Pilots will now climb on top of its hull, open a compartment and steal a battery that can be used to add a shield to their own Titan or a teammate’s. This mechanic can be incredibly useful during heated Titan battles, and it adds a strategic layer to the fight, as a talented Pilot can steal an enemy Titan’s battery just in time to save a teammate from certain death in a way that wasn’t really possible in the first Titanfall.

Another big change is the removal of customizable Titans in favor of a class system in which players can choose from six different archetypes who all sport different weapons and abilities. This makes them feel like MOBA heroes or hero shooter characters, as every one of them has a signature ultimate ability that can be unleashed upon the enemy as the core progression meter reaches 100%. Of course, even though the new Titan classes can’t be customized in terms of weaponry or skills, gamers can still choose different skins, making each machine slightly different from the rest.

The progression system has been overhauled as well, and there are a lot more weapons and customization options to be earned as players level up, something that will definitely help the game on the long run.

Titanfall 2 shines on the tech department as well, as it not only looks gorgeous (it’s hard to believe that this game runs on Valve‘s Source engine) but it also runs like a dream. Voice acting is perfect, as we said before, and both the sound effects and the soundtrack fit the title perfectly, with chunky hit sounds giving the right feedback as bullets hit their targets, and catchy tunes playing just when the situation needs them.

To conclude, Titanfall 2 is one of the best shooters released in the past decade. Respawn Entertainment mixed an unforgettable singleplayer campaign with an excellent multiplayer suite, creating the ultimate action package, something that every FPS fan worth their salt should at least try (and while we are at it, the Stream re-release has revitalized the playerbase, so multiplayer matches are easy to find. Get in there, Pilot!)

Honestly, this game is truly underrated. That 2009–2016 era of FPS games was something special, and coming back to Titanfall 2 just reminds me how unmatched it really was. The combat is slick and incredibly fluid, movement just feels great even if a little floaty. I’m still not the biggest fan of some of the guns (a few lean a bit too hard into sci fi gimmick territory for me with a few interesting ones I wont lie), but the moment to moment gameplay more than makes up for it. The story isn’t the most original premise you’ll ever see, but it never tries to be anything it isn’t. It’s confident, tight, and surprisingly heartfelt. The banter with BT hits that perfect balance of dry humour, warmth, and weight a nice emotional break from the game’s overall darker tone. It's genuinely one of the better buddy dynamic narratives in shooters. And the level design? Honestly incredible. There are moments here that feel like master class set pieces taking advantage of unique mechanics in ways that are memorable without feeling like gimmicks. Levels like that one (you know the one) are still talked about for a reason, and even outside the standout moments, the campaign’s pacing and creativity keep things constantly engaging. It's got some decent performances by its voice actors which is always appreciated. It’s short, punchy, and doesn’t waste your time a rare thing now. Titanfall 2 really deserved better support and recognition at launch, because even today it stands toe to toe with the best shooters ever made.

Important Note: Don’t buy this game in the Titanfall Collection bundle that comes with the first Titanfall, at the time I’m writing this review Titanfall 1’s servers are still down due to hackers, meaning the game is 100% unplayable even though it’s still being sold full price on Steam, from what I've heard this problem has been going on for 3 years + and still hasn't been addressed at all. Titanfall 2 is just fine though and still has a thriving online community from my experience (I’ve heard of others having server/hacker problems with TF2, but personally I never had issues getting into lobbies and never found any hackers in 50+ hours of multiplayer, so I can’t recommend against the game because of that risk if I never experienced it personally), so for sure get it on its own, just don’t buy Titanfall 1 unless you hear they fixed the servers (which Respawn did promise to do, but that was several months ago, so who knows if they really plan to go through with sorting out these issues in the long run).

More info on these issues can be found here: https://www.rockpapershotgun.com/the-first-titanfall-arrives-on-steam-utterly-broken, https://savetitanfall.com/whats-happening-to-titanfall-2

Update: Respawn have been working on TF1 after all, I bought it and played a bunch of matches recently with no issues, how long this will last for is anyone's guess but clearly they are making moves to squash these hacker problems, took much longer than it should have but credit to them for coming back to an old game like this.

Pros
- Singleplayer campaign. One of the biggest strengths of Titanfall 2 for me is that it has a full scale singleplayer story mode, the “campaign” in Titanfall 1 was a series of online multiplayer matches with narration over the top and cutscenes before them, TF2 on the other hand has a 9 mission campaign with maps specifically built for it, offering up a good mix of Titan and Pilot gameplay, combat and platforming and including lots of different scripted sequences and gimmicks to keep things interesting throughout, the story is solid and the relationship between your player character and their Titan really stands out, it’s a bond you stick with and get committed to.
- Smooth movement. As a Pilot movement is really fast paced and traversing around the maps with a combo of sprinting, wall running, boost jumping and flinging yourself around with the grapple hook feels amazing, going from A to B at breakneck speed has never been so fun.
- Excellent multiplayer.  The combat in TF2 is competitive and exciting, there’s a solid variety of weapons to use (Primary Weapons like Rifles, SMGs, Snipers, Shotguns, Sidearms aka Pistols and Revolvers and purpose built Anti-Titan Weapons: Energy Weapons, Rocket and Grenade Launchers), lots of different abilities to equip (cloaking, grapple, phase shift, etc etc) and you can pick from several different classes of Titan to use each with their own weaponry and abilities. There’s a healthy balancing act between Pilots and Titans, a skilled Pilot player can easily zip around and destroy Titans in David v Goliath acts with special Anti-Titan guns, a skilled Titan player can rip enemy teams to shreds with their high powered gear, the fast time to kill of Pilot vs Pilot combat also contrasts nicely with the slow TTK of Titan v Titan fighting.

Cons
- Campaign is short. All the missions in the campaign feel well done and enjoyable, but they’re fairly short and easy to beat, the campaign doesn’t last longer than 6 hours or so in total, it feels like it could’ve had a few more missions included to be properly fulfilling.
- Occasional unbalanced matchmaking. This isn’t really a fault of the game, just a consequence of the small playerbase, but since there’s not a huge community for the game any more you can sometimes end up in wildly unbalanced lobbies either going up against an elite team way more experienced than you which gives you a thorough curb stomping, with your brothers in arms all being low level new players or vice versa, ending up with a super OP team and stomping out the enemy without them having a fair shot at a win, most matches I’ve gotten into have been fair and workable but sometimes you end up in borderline unwinnable scenarios because the teams don’t have a good mix of new and experienced players each.
- Lacking game mode variety on MP. Again, not really the game’s fault, but due to the small community it’s very hard to find matches in any mode other than Team Deathmatch (aka Attrition), Attrition is the mode everyone’s still playing for the most part so you’ll almost never have any luck getting a game in another mode unless you sit in matchmaking for hours on end or get lucky.

Honestly I think that Titanfall 2 is one of the best shooters of its generation, it’s what the boost jumping Call of Duty games (Advanced Warfare, Black Ops 3, Infinite Warfare, etc) should have been, really smooth fast paced movement and stellar gunplay combined with a really interesting setting. The Campaign is worth a run or two and that can make up around 6-12 hours or so of your time and while the Multiplayer community is small (averaging roughly 4000-10,000 players online every day) it’s still very active and matchmaking is fast as long as you don’t mind only playing Attrition most of the time, MP has a ton of unlocks to get and milestones to reach and its something you can sink thousands of hours into if you choose to stick with it (I ended up getting 30+ hours in Multiplayer in my first few days of getting the game because I got so hooked). I really enjoyed the first Titanfall when it came out and 2 improves on that game in more or less every area imaginable, I just cannot recommend this game enough, it’s nearly 5 years old now yet it still holds up 100% today, if you enjoy competitive MP shooters you really should give it a try.

I can't believe EA almost made me miss this masterpiece.

The campaign lasted ~7 hours and that's the only complaint I have about this game.
I usually do a 'pros' and 'cons' but for this one, it can only be 'amazing' and 'good'.

Amazing:
- Animations - so well crafted and carefully detailed.
- Gunplay - every gun feels good, especially the ones for the Titan.
- Mech piloting - easy to understand and so satisfying. 
- Music - fits every scene.

Good:
- Writing/dialog - the way the story/bond flows between BT and Cooper is amazing considering the campaign length and the dialog overall is not over-the-top and funny in just the right amount.
- AI - for the bosses especially.
- Level design - so good in the factory and some wall running places.
- Mechanics - not innovative but the combination is really good.

It's truly one of the best FPS of all time.

Just about the campaign:

It's like those seventh gen campaigns inspired by the hideous popularity of Call of Duty games. Super linear, very short, overscripted and committed to relentlessly presenting stupid popcorn cinematic blockbuster action in which thinking, breathing and acting on your own was considered a crime. Canned in a package with great production values, extreme polish and stories chewy enough to be digested by an infant.

That's what Titanfall 2's campaign is. But good. 

If CoD campaigns were creative, well-inspired, and replayable, they would be like this campaign.

It's a tight compilation of very well-made levels, a little more open and immensely more creative and fun to play thanks to the expanded moveset and the very friendly and charming talking robot that shoots missiles and has a flamethrower. 

The pace is close to perfection and the freshness never ends because it's a game that never stops throwing curveballs and surprising you with new ideas until the end of its short duration. Everything is given time to breathe, develop and then be replaced by the next crazy concept, without ever abandoning the very solid and well-balanced movement and combat mechanics.

The level of action in this game is simply sublime. Perfectly dosed, chaotic, exciting and modestly challenging, without being too demanding. 

Depending on the situation, you could even say that there is some level of depth and strategy involved in the  shooting.

And best of all? The game isn't just about that. It's not just about moving forward and grinding out endless hordes of convenient stereotypes. There is a good dose of exploration and traversal challenges, and a combination of these elements.

They definitely nailed the dynamic between controlling the titan and playing with boots on the ground(Or on the walls), and the balance between the quiet times that generate immersion and the bombastic action sequences that puts any blockbuster to shame.

And there's even a fun story, with a enduring chemistry between you and your robotic friend. 

All the one-liners you want are here, being thrown at the most memorable moments. As it should be.

Graphics, sound, music, and the like, leave nothing to be desired. This is a top-notch presentation.

Titanfall 2 is nothing short of a gem in the world of first-person shooters, blending fluid mechanics, engaging storytelling, and thrilling mech-based combat into one unforgettable package. Released in 2016, it stands as a testament to how innovation in game design can produce something truly special. However, despite its brilliance, the game now faces challenges in its multiplayer landscape, largely due to being overshadowed by its battle royale sibling, Apex Legends.

[h1]Campaign: A Perfectly Executed Storyline[/h1]
One of the standout features of Titanfall 2 is its campaign mode, which is widely regarded as one of the best in FPS history. The story revolves around Jack Cooper, a humble rifleman who unexpectedly forms a bond with a Vanguard-class Titan, BT-7274, after his pilot is killed in action. Their journey together is emotional, exciting, and filled with clever twists. The dynamic between Jack and BT brings heart to the narrative, making the story more than just a vehicle for the action.
Each mission introduces new mechanics that keep the gameplay fresh, from wall-running platforming challenges to time-travel puzzles. The creativity behind these sequences ensures that every level feels unique, culminating in a finale that will leave you in awe.

[h1]Gameplay: Smooth, Fast, and Addictive[/h1]
Titanfall 2's gameplay is its crown jewel. The movement mechanics are unmatched, offering fast-paced wall-running, double-jumping, and parkour-like traversal that feels incredibly fluid and rewarding. Whether you’re darting across walls in a tight gunfight or dropping into a Titan from orbit, the gameplay never stops being exhilarating.
The combat offers a seamless blend of infantry and mech-based gameplay. Titans, the giant mechanized war machines, add a layer of strategy to the combat. Each Titan comes with unique abilities and playstyles, ensuring there’s something for everyone. Pilots and Titans complement each other perfectly, making every battle feel dynamic and intense.

[h1]Multiplayer: A Double-Edged Sword[/h1]
Titanfall 2’s multiplayer was revolutionary at launch, providing chaotic and action-packed matches where players could seamlessly switch between Pilots and Titans. Modes like Attrition and Last Titan Standing kept players hooked with a mix of tactical and frenetic gameplay. The progression system, customization options, and map designs were all top-notch.
Unfortunately, time has not been kind to Titanfall 2’s multiplayer. With the rise of Apex Legends, Respawn Entertainment’s wildly popular battle royale game, Titanfall 2's servers have become much less active. It’s a sad reality that this incredible multiplayer experience has been largely abandoned by the player base, leaving many matches sparsely populated or difficult to find. For a game that thrives on competitive energy, this lack of activity is a noticeable drawback.

[h1]Graphics and Sound Design: A Feast for the Senses[/h1]
Visually, Titanfall 2 still holds up beautifully, even years after its release. The environments are diverse and detailed, ranging from lush forests to industrial war zones. The Titans themselves are intricately designed, showcasing their power and scale.
The sound design is equally impressive. The heavy footsteps of a Titan, the crackling of energy weapons, and the atmospheric music all combine to immerse players in the game’s sci-fi universe. It’s a sensory experience that feels both grand and intimate.

[h1]Final Thoughts[/h1]
Titanfall 2 is a masterclass in first-person shooter design. Its innovative gameplay, heartfelt campaign, and exhilarating multiplayer make it one of the finest FPS games of its generation. However, the decline in multiplayer activity and the rise of Apex Legends have left this incredible game underappreciated by newer audiences.
If you haven’t experienced Titanfall 2 yet, it’s a must-play for the campaign alone. It’s a love letter to innovation in gaming, and for those lucky enough to find a multiplayer match, it’s a reminder of what peak FPS multiplayer can look like. Whether you’re new to the series or a returning fan, Titanfall 2 deserves your attention, it’s a game that truly deserves to stand tall, even if its servers are quiet.

Titanfall 2 is a fast paced shooter with extremely fun gameplay, beautifully crafted levels and some interesting mechanics.
You're a soldier who finds the titan of his fallen brethren and becomes one with it. You and your titan start binding with each other, knowing each other and becoming not only partners but friends. Nothing special, just a simple story about a boy and his titan but it's told very well. There's not a lot dialogues or cut-scenes. Story is uncovered by dialogues while playing. This game is really similar to CoD, a CoD game with robots to be precise. That's not a bad thing.

The fun part is the gameplay. It's fast and it's fun as hell. You control either the titan and you sit inside of it or your character on foot. Usually you control the titan in open locations and the main character only in closed environments. Basically waves of enemies spawn around and try to kill you and you must use your arsenal to kill them. You can jump, land on them and punch them or go invisible and stab them from the back or just shoot them all to the face. The combat is very fluid and action is rarely interrupted. While inside your titan you feel invincible, especially when killing simple foot soldiers, it's like crushing ants. But there are tough sections too where you fight bosses who are bad guys with their own titans.
There's one interesting mechanic – you can run on walls and jump from one wall to another to go where you want. Some of these platforming sections could be a bit tricky but it's still fun. Other than that it's a nicely done shooter with very satisfying gameplay which is full of non-stop action.

There's a multiplayer, it's a fast paced shooter very similar to CoD, only you can summon the titan for limited time. I'm not into multiplayer, but I guess this should be extremely fun for CoD fans and those who don't care about teamplay, tactics etc, just point your gun, shoot, jump, die, repeat.

Graphics are pleasantly surprising. Although the game is few years old it still looks very good. Every area is quite unique and feels fresh. Gameplay is changing depending on the mission so there's no repetitiveness at all.
Performance is flawless, should run on potatoes too.

If you're getting this for the campaign then save your money and get EA play instead. The game is very short (~5 hours) and isn't worth the price. If you're interested in multiplayer and you love fast shooters then it's definitely worth a buy.

For a long time I've been hearing from other people "PLAY TITANFALL 2", and I was all "Well I don't want to install a whole other digital store just to play one thing" and they'd respond with "PLAY TITANFALL 2". The game got released on Steam and having played it myself I will now join the chorus of people yelling in all caps "PLAY TITANFALL 2"

Normally I wouldn't be into a shooter like this with such a quick time to death, but the movement adds fun new layers of tech to the shooter formula that's been dominated by the CoD franchise to make Titanfall stand out. Wall running lets the player reach speed that cannot be reached by regular running around. The double jump and climbing allows the maps to have lots of verticality and gives the player multiple options to get to where they want to go. When running the crouch becomes a slide, letting the player swooce into cover if getting shot at, allowing them to zip under small gaps, and turning melee attacks into uppercuts.

Weapon wise there's a lot to work with, all the staples are here and there should be something for everyone. Shotguns, SMGs, rifles, machine guns, energy weapons, even stuff that shoots projectiles you need to lead instead of the hitscan weapons that you'd expect. Multiple grenade types as well, so there's plenty of things to mess around with until you mix and match your way to finding exactly what works best for you. Personally I'm a fan of the energy machine gun that makes people explode like hotdogs in a microwave and the thermite ninja stars.

Then we get to the titans themselves. In multiplayer you build your way towards earning one (in the modes where there are titans) by fighting, and they're pretty good rewards for doing so. They completely change how you play, you can kill players outside of titans just by stepping on them, the UI changes, you lose options for movement and are too big to get into smaller spaces, but you get new tricks in return. Each titan model has different guns, different skills, and a different super move that they can do if they live long enough to earn it, and a different look (that you can customize further with skins and nose art and stuff), so each one is pretty unique. Though titans are harder to kill than regular pilots, pilots have their own stuff to even the odds as well: anti-titan secondary weapons such as RPGs or laser cannons, and you can jump on enemy titans to steal batteries and deal damage, and jump on friendly titans to prevent the same thing from happening to your team, and to give batteries you stole.

Multiplayer is still active, despite the games age, I never had to wait too long to get into a match, and there's plenty of different mods to mess around with. While there are max level "John Titanfall" players who've been around since the game was originally released I never ran into too many, so that wasn't that big of a deal for me. The community isn't that bad, there's some shit talking but I never ran into "XBOX live lobby" levels of pre-teen screeching.

I did have to install some version of Origin to gets this going which I didn't like, but I don't think this was going to come to Steam otherwise.

After all these years, it’s still the best first-person shooter by a huge margin.
I can’t believe people prefer to play the same repetitive Call of Duty or Battlefield games with no special gameplay or story, while a masterpiece like Titanfall 2 is collecting dust—just because EA was stupid enough to destroy their only masterpiece with their own hands.

Even after losing this game, they’re now losing Apex as well. With simple ideas—like adding Jack Cooper as a character in Apex, or even just releasing a few skins for Titanfall 2—they could have kept the community alive. But instead, they decided to focus on Battlefield and their other useless games.

If you’re interested, read this review from me, a young FPS gamer who’s been playing shooters for almost 10 years.

Gameplay
The core gameplay of Titanfall 2 is a masterpiece. Not because it was the first game to combine this kind of movement with an FPS, but because it did it in the best possible way.
This movement system doesn’t add any disadvantages—it only improves the experience.

The campaign missions are incredible, combining amazing level design with masterful gunplay and movement. The online gameplay was so good that Apex later took many of its mechanics, and other shooters copied elements of it too. It’s a joy to see that there are still skilled players keeping the online alive.

The gameplay truly showcases what a masterpiece looks like.

Story
The story is genuinely engaging. Jack Cooper starts as just an ordinary soldier, and the plot develops in a way that turns him into the pilot of BT-7274. But what really shines is the evolution of the bond between the two.

Earlier, BT even tells Cooper about his long relationship with Captain Tai Lastimosa, and we realize that the bond between pilots and their Titans is not ordinary at all. The way this relationship develops is beautiful. Cooper clearly doesn’t know anything about being a pilot at first, and the dialogue reflects that. But together, they learn. BT becomes a true friend, and Cooper becomes a true pilot.

Just as BT’s first lines explain the protocols, his final lines end with the same—and with that unforgettable “Trust me.” I’m sure no one has ever felt such emotions for a robot before.

Issues
Aside from the campaign being short, my biggest problem was the weak boss fights. Except for Viper—who was absolutely amazing—the others were weak, almost indistinguishable from fighting a normal Titan. But still, when you defeat Ash, you get that satisfying feeling of victory.

Final Thoughts
I bought this game for 5 dollars, and it feels like I committed a sin. The game is absolutely beautiful, and you enjoy every moment of it. The campaign is amazing, and the multiplayer is still alive even today.

Definitely buy this game if it’s on sale—it’s absolutely worth it.

Titanfall 2 is a perfect sequel. It really is. The developers listened to our feedback and improved on absolutely everything. The result? A modern masterpiece! I remember playing Titanfall 2 back in 2016 and thinking "This is it. This is peak online shooting. It can't get much better than this." Do I still think this is true? Definitely. Multiplayer is not the only reason why the game is great though.The campaign is excellent as well. Sure it only took me five hours to beat the campaign on hard but it was a brilliant ride.
Let me put it this way: I rather pay 49.99€ for a great 5h long campaign than a 20h long slog.

The story itself is quite decent. It has a few pleasant surprises here and there. The pacing is perfect and the action... Oh my, the action! The campaign throws perfect wall-running, sliding,
shooting, jumping, mech action, puzzle-solving, and exploring sections in your face and absolutely every single one of those sections is marvelously designed, wonderfully paced and just a joy to play. 
At first, you might think Titanfall 2 is another ordinary military shooter with the addition of wall-running and mech control but that simply isn't true. As I already mentioned the game throws platforming and puzzle sections at you as well.
The story itself does have a couple of twists in it and it's not just humans you have to battle. There are different monsters, people, robots, mini-mechs, huge mechs, boss mechs, and harsh environments you have to navigate yourself in.
I have to admit I was falling to my death more often than I'd like to admit and definitely died more due to failing jumps than getting unalived in combat.

Now let's talk about multiplayer.
Right off the bat, I want to say there is also a co-op mode that doesn't get enough credit and
people never mention it in their reviews.
It is pretty straightforward: Four players must work together and survive five waves of enemies.

PvP is what interests you the most though, right? It's incredible! Have you ever seen any of the Call of Duty, Battlefield, Apex, or any other multiplayer trailer for a game? The trailers look intense but you never see anything like that in the real game. You rarely get any of those epic trailer moments in your average multiplayer match.
Titanfall 2 is the exact opposite. No trailer does it justice. Every match you make, every breath you take, is a ballet of an action hero.
Call in your titan while wall-running, double jump towards the titan that just landed, and squashed your opponents. The titan grabs you mid-air and together you rock 'n' roll to blow
everything up. It's brilliant, smooth, simple to execute, and satisfying.

What modes can you play? I hear you ask. You have your classic team deathmatches, capture the flag, free-for-all, domination-like mode, and a couple of more deathmatch modes with different rules. Oh, and in case anyone is wondering: Yes. The multiplayer is very much alive.

Conclusion: Titanfall 2 has more than enough content to justify the price. It is a perfectly executed game and a worthy sequel.
It's unique, beautiful, and will satisfy both single-player and competitive players alike.
It's definitely worth your hard-earned money.

Titanfall 2 remains an exceptional example of how a first-person shooter can combine fluid movement, satisfying weapons, creative level design, memorable characters, and large-scale mechanical combat without allowing any single element to overshadow the others. Developed by Respawn Entertainment and published by Electronic Arts, it offers both a carefully designed single-player campaign and competitive multiplayer. Its defining idea is the contrast between extremely agile Pilots and heavily armed Titans, creating two distinct styles of combat that complement each other remarkably well.

The campaign follows Jack Cooper, a Militia rifleman who finds himself stranded behind enemy lines and unexpectedly partnered with BT-7274, a Vanguard-class Titan. What initially appears to be a straightforward military science-fiction story gradually develops into a surprisingly engaging partnership. BT's logical, literal personality provides plenty of understated humor, while Cooper's growing trust in his mechanical companion gives the campaign an emotional foundation. Their relationship never overwhelms the action, but it gives purpose to the battles and makes important story moments considerably more memorable.

Movement is arguably the game's greatest accomplishment. Cooper can sprint, slide, double-jump and wall-run, allowing environments to function as elaborate traversal playgrounds rather than ordinary shooter corridors. Chaining these abilities together creates an exhilarating sense of momentum. Once the mechanics become familiar, simply moving from one location to another becomes entertaining. Combat benefits enormously from this mobility because staying stationary is rarely the most enjoyable approach. Players can rush along walls, leap over enemies, slide beneath obstacles and fire while constantly repositioning.

The gunplay is equally responsive. Weapons have satisfying feedback and cover enough different styles to encourage experimentation, but their effectiveness is enhanced by the movement system. Instead of repeatedly hiding behind cover and exchanging fire from fixed positions, players are encouraged to attack aggressively and use vertical space. Encounters can become fast, almost acrobatic sequences where traversal and shooting blend naturally together. The result is an FPS that rewards both accuracy and an understanding of momentum.

Titan combat provides a deliberate contrast. Entering BT or another Titan changes the player's perspective from vulnerable but extraordinarily mobile infantry to a towering armored machine. Titan battles emphasize positioning, defensive abilities, powerful weapons and knowledge of enemy capabilities. Different Titan configurations support different approaches, preventing mechanical combat from becoming a simple contest of durability. Despite their enormous strength, Titans do not make Pilot gameplay irrelevant, which is crucial to maintaining the balance between the game's two major combat styles.

The campaign's level design deserves particular praise because it constantly introduces new situations rather than repeatedly recycling the same formula. Platforming challenges, environmental hazards, large battlefields, mechanical puzzles and inventive gameplay concepts regularly change the rhythm. Some stages introduce mechanics strong enough that another game might have built its entire campaign around them, yet here they are used for a focused section before another idea takes their place. This approach keeps the adventure consistently fresh and gives individual missions distinct identities.

Multiplayer takes the movement and Titan mechanics into a much more demanding environment. Human opponents understand verticality, wall-running and rapid repositioning, producing matches that can become extraordinarily fast. Pilots can appear from rooftops, walls, windows or unexpected angles, while the arrival of Titans dramatically changes the battlefield. The mixture of infantry and mechanical combat creates a distinctive competitive identity that separates it from shooters built around conventional ground movement.

Customization adds another layer to multiplayer. Players can experiment with Pilot abilities, weapons, equipment and Titan choices while developing loadouts suited to their preferred style. The different Titan types offer meaningful variations rather than functioning merely as cosmetic alternatives. Some approaches favor direct aggression, while others reward range, positioning, defensive play or careful ability management. This variety gives players plenty of opportunities to find combinations matching their strengths.

Visually, the game continues to benefit from strong artistic direction. Industrial complexes, futuristic military installations, wilderness areas and enormous mechanical structures provide varied backdrops while simultaneously supporting the movement system. Environments are designed with walls, platforms and vertical pathways that encourage traversal rather than merely decorating the battlefield. Audio contributes heavily to the sense of power as well. Firearms sound forceful, explosions carry weight, and Titan machinery convincingly communicates the enormous scale of these machines.

The campaign does have limitations. Its strongest ideas sometimes disappear almost as quickly as they are introduced, leaving the player wishing certain mechanics had been explored further. The story is effective but relatively straightforward outside the Cooper and BT relationship. Multiplayer also presents a substantial learning curve because experienced players can use advanced movement techniques to cross maps and attack from unexpected directions with intimidating speed. Beginners should expect some difficult matches while learning how traversal and combat work together.

The Steam version additionally requires interaction with EA's account and online infrastructure, which introduces an unnecessary layer between launching the game and actually playing it. It does not ruin the underlying experience, but players who prefer completely self-contained Steam titles may find the additional account requirement inconvenient.

Steam Deck compatibility is more complicated than the game's controller-friendly mechanics might suggest. It does not currently carry an official Steam Deck compatibility rating from Valve. Community reports indicate that the game itself can run well on the handheld and its controller-based movement translates naturally to portable play, but the required EA launcher can introduce complications. Launcher updates, authentication requirements and occasional compatibility issues can affect an otherwise capable handheld experience. Players primarily interested in Steam Deck play should therefore expect that some troubleshooting may occasionally be necessary rather than assuming a seamless console-like experience.

Ultimately, the game succeeds because virtually every major system contributes to a consistent feeling of speed, freedom and power. Pilot movement is exceptionally responsive, Titan battles provide satisfying heavyweight combat, the campaign continually experiments with new ideas, and the relationship between Cooper and BT gives the adventure genuine personality. Multiplayer further demonstrates how much mechanical depth exists beneath the accessible controls. Even years after its original arrival, few shooters combine parkour, precision gunplay and mech warfare with comparable confidence. It is an outstanding choice for anyone who values inventive FPS campaigns and fast, skill-driven action.
